items.title: Gary Anderson's verdict on McLaren's 2027-leaning upgrade
items.author: Gary Anderson
items.content:
No team wants to show its dirty washing in public, so McLaren calling its new front wing effectively a 2027 concept seems strange.

In that position, assuming the numbers on track and the simulation tools show it has potential, I’d be using it now and considering it very much a 2026 part. With (perhaps) four races remaining and roughly five months before the start of next season, I’d be learning as much as possible from it and would hopefully make a step or two as a result of it before next season kicks off.

The intersection between the mainplane and the lower foot of the endplate, highlighted with the red ellipse, is what caught my eye.

Red Bull started the season with this concept, and Mercedes and others have followed. Making it more of a single lower surface reduces the sensitivity of the endplate footplate to the track, so in high-speed corners the front of the car should produce more consistent downforce. Basically, it should feel less snatchy, making the rear of the car more stable.

The slot gap profile between the forward and central elements, highlighted with the green arrow, has also been altered.

This is in line with the profile change highlighted with the light blue arrow and the positioning of the longest chord section of the third element. With that section slightly more inboard, this will alter where the mass flow reaches the leading edge of the floor.

What confuses me a little is the change from reducing the angle of the second and third elements in straight mode to reducing only the angle of the third when straight mode is activated. It means that the front wing is less powerful in corner mode, but that comes at the expense of overall downforce.

When the wing is in cornering mode (max downforce), the low pressure on the lower surface will pull more of its airflow through the slot gap between the first and second elements. To compensate for this, McLaren has reduced the chord length of the mainplane, highlighted with the green arrow, and increased the chord length of the second element, highlighted with the light blue arrow.

Mounting the wing on the second element, as highlighted with the red ellipse is sensible with this concept as it’s the best stiffness-to-weight compromise, but only if you don’t use the mid-flap as part of the straight-line mode wing angle reduction. So perhaps that, together with the fact that the car seems to be struggling with the balance between low- to medium-speed corners and high-speed corners, has led McLaren to this concept.

There are also small additions to the rear wing trailing edge, highlighted with the green arrows. I can’t really see enough to tell if it’s a completely new package, but I’ve highlighted the small additions. These will improve the airflow on the wing’s underside, which is affected by the twin mounting pillars. A small airflow separation problem behind those mountings can very easily spread across a much wider section of the wing’s underside.McLaren has also declared a new diffuser and a re-profiled rear beam wing.

This year the beam wing has a much shorter chord than in previous seasons, but it’s still very powerful when it comes to improving the performance of the diffuser. I don’t have the visual information to go into much detail on the diffuser.

It’s basically the component that has a major influence on the overall performance of the car, so teams tend to keep these components well hidden.

"The upgrades, even though I had half and then half, and we’re going to put everything together for tomorrow, the upgrades seem to have given what we hoped for, I would say," was Lando Norris's early verdict on Friday.

"Ultimately, the upgrades are there to bring laptime and bring performance. They’re not set out just to improve handling. A perfect upgrade is one that brings laptime and at the same time brings a handling upgrade, especially with how tricky the car’s been. 

"I would say maybe there’s a small change in the right direction; it seems just a little bit more straightforward to drive.

"But I don’t think we can ever judge things over just one track. But so far, for today, things have seemed a little bit more straightforward, which is a good thing."

Let’s see how it all performs when it matters on Saturday and Sunday and if McLaren keeps all these components on the car as the weekend progresses.

items.title: Herta finally clears his last F1 superlicence hurdle
items.author: Scott Mitchell-Malm
items.content:
Colton Herta has cleared the final hurdles to qualifying for a Formula 1 superlicence with his penalty-free and productive Friday practice outing for Cadillac at the Brazilian Grand Prix.

Herta replaced Sergio Perez in FP1 at Interlagos, where he and Cadillac were seeking to seal the final point needed for Herta to be eligible for a superlicence.

He is a contender to race for the team next season but even if 2027 comes too soon getting a superlicence now would also make it much easier for Herta to remain an option in the years that follow, too.

A driver needs to accrue 40 superlicence points when applying for the first time. Cadillac thought this had already been achieved after his Mexico FP1 appearance a week ago, but Herta was still one short after a mix-up over a previous IndyCar result.

He was immediately back in the car for Brazil to seal the deal, though, so long as he completed 100km and did not get any penalty points on his licence in the session.

Herta could have been tripped up on either count. The red flag that emerged early in FP1 could have shortened running significantly enough that he did not do enough laps for it to count – and it also caused a brief scare when Herta went past the pit entry after the session had been red-flagged.

No action was taken as it was clear the red light panels came on too late for him to react and get into the pitlane.

Cadillac’s Marc Hynes said on Friday evening that the team wanted to be absolutely clear whether the 100km limit comes from total mileage or only mileage from timed laps, but either way Herta would be safe.

The Race understands the FIA is satisfied with what he did in FP1 so the superlicence point will be earned and his eligibility will be confirmed in due course.

Herta ran a full programme in FP1 with early laps on hard tyres hampered by some lock-ups before a switch to softs, which yielded a best lap 0.904s slower than Valtteri Bottas over one lap and 0.275s slower than the target Cadillac set him.

Herta was due to speak to media at the end of the day but withdrew from those activities as Cadillac said he was feeling unwell.

When Hynes spoke, though, he said Herta was making good progress with his F1 work dovetailed alongside a disappointing Formula 2 campaign in which he is only 19th in the standings.

"It was a huge step to come to Europe chasing the F1 dream, and I hugely admire that," Hynes said.

"F2 is difficult. You’ve got the guys that have come through in the same peer set from karting, they know all the tracks – you get very little mileage in F2 practice, they know the tyre very well, and the driving style is baked in. So to come into that is tough.

"FP1 is a good opportunity to get some mileage, and he’s got better every time. The nerves aren’t there that you have for the first one, and he’s really looking assured out there now."

items.title: Winners & losers from F1 2026 Brazilian GP Friday practice
items.author: Ben Anderson
items.content:
A familiar name at the top of the timesheet, but not your run of the mill F1 Friday at the Brazilian Grand Prix, as one struggling frontrunner got back in the groove again while the usual kings of Friday practice produced their worst result of the season.

Here are our winners and losers from the first day of F1 track action at Interlagos.

Loser: Ferrari (6th & 7th)

Charles Leclerc and Ferrari had been fastest in Friday practice at three of the past four races, going back to October’s Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, and a 6-7 FP2 result in Brazil (with Leclerc behind Lewis Hamilton) was the first time all season Ferrari has finished Friday outside the top five on the timesheet.

Leclerc called it a “very, very difficult Friday” and described the feeling inside the car as “strange” and “very poor”.

“We were losing in the straights, but I think the car in the corners just felt probably one of the worst Friday feelings of the season," he added.

“So I think there's a lot to be found in corners, more than in the straights, where we know we have a deficit. Normally we are very fast in corners and today was not the case.”

Team boss Fred Vasseur joked this was a Friday when Ferrari “have 200 kilos” of fuel inside the cars in order to flip the script, such is their usually prodigious form in free practice, but in a serious moment then admitted Ferrari has “a lot of work to do on the balance”.

“The drivers, they were not happy,” he confirmed, while also saying he was “not less optimistic than last week” when Leclerc topped Friday in Mexico.

“We had a couple of times a deployment issue in the lap,” Vasseur added. “We have to fine-tune everything.

“On his fastest lap, he [Leclerc] lost a couple of tenths in a straight line. I would say that it’s not a drama. It’s more for you [the media] to be focused on page one [of the timing screen], but we are not.

“We know that we have a lot to do on the balance. The balance was not good. The tarmac is the opposite of one week ago. It’s creating a lot of work to do and a difference compared to last week.” -

Winner: McLaren (2nd & 5th)

Fastest in FP1 and looking competitive on longer runs - McLaren's upgrade package for Brazil appears to be working well, with the usual caveat that Fridays don't always offer perfect insight into the order.

Senior racing director Randy Singh said it's "very likely" the upgrades - led by a new front wing - will stay on the car, and Friday went "really well" for the team, while Lando Norris cautioned that the team still looks two-tenths off Kimi Antonelli's Mercedes but "pretty good" compared to the other teams.

Norris also felt gently encouraged that McLaren's new 2027-ethos front wing had begun to address the long-standing edginess of the car's balance.

"I would say maybe there’s a small change in the right direction, that it seems just a little bit more straightforward to drive," he said.

"I don’t think we can ever judge things over just one track. But so far, for today, things have seemed a little bit more straightforward."

After missing FP1, Singh says Oscar Piastri was also "immediately on the pace" - something which hasn't always happened this year - but the usual rule from recent races applies: the team needs to optimise qualifying, where its knife-edge car has let its long-run pace down all too often. -

Winner: Gabriele Mini (7th in FP1)

Every now and then, a lesser-known Friday driver pops up high on the timesheets in an FP1 outing, which is exactly what Gabriele Mini did on his second appearance for Alpine by setting the seventh-fastest time to head the midfield pack. 

"Gabby did a very good job to be a little bit quicker than his team-mate," said Alpine managing director Steve Nielsen.

"[It's the] second weekend in a row for him and he looks like a seasoned campaigner already. He literally didn't put a foot wrong, which is really good."

The 21-year-old Italian, when he wasn't reading from the standard FP1 driver script about focusing on doing a good job for the team, showed that he wasn't keen to rest on his laurels after making a positive impression and admitted to areas where he knew his lap, quick as it was, could have been better. 

"There were a few things that, let’s say, didn’t allow me to make the best lap," said Mini when asked by The Race to break down his lap.

"The lap of your life, it’s really hard to get in an FP1, but where I had some margin was in corners like Turn 1, because there was never a clear run before the actual push, so I never really had an idea, so I took a bit of margin there, which I know I have. 

"And then some other corners, a bit in the braking points, some slides that I got that could have been better. It’s hard to really say how much time. I don’t [say] one second, but for sure a few tenths are easy.

"Something that we could have done better with the switches as well, so not only my side. But that’s something that, as I said, you get in FP1 to then improve in FP2, both driver- and engineer-wise. So it’s normal to have those kinds of things, I’d say."

Mini, who was a star name in his karting career and has since won the 2020 Italian F4 title and races at every level up to and including F2, has shown that not only is he quick but also determined to improve.

And those are two key prerequisites of a potential F1 race driver. -

Loser: Anyone hoping Kimi Antonelli would switch off...

For anyone unfamiliar with old English idioms, something ‘after the Lord Mayor’s Show’ is a classic expression to describe something mundane, or disappointment following something much grander – like, for instance, a bog-standard F1 Friday for Kimi Antonelli five days after winning the world championship!

But anyone hoping Antonelli would be switching off with some kind of post-title hangover will be sorely disappointed by how he breezed through practice at Interlagos with all his rivals at arm’s length.

"It’s the next Lord Mayor’s show for him, not the after," said Mercedes deputy team principal Bradley Lord.

"There’s two big things. We’ve got our constructors’ championship to win and a job to complete, and both drivers are really determined to do that, to translate and recognise the effort of everyone back in Brixworth and in Brackley.

"And then this is the start of 2027 for Kimi, and he’s determined to finish the season on a high, but take that momentum through into the winter."

There is no hint of complacency, change in mindset, or relaxing off the gas for the new world champion.

Without him, Mercedes would have looked right in the mix against McLaren and Red Bull, but nothing more. With Antonelli it heads into Saturday as the pole favourite - if the weather doesn’t change, of course. -

Winner: Colton Herta (20th in FP1)

It looks like Colton Herta has really, genuinely, finally done it – he qualifies for an F1 superlicence, in one of the most unnecessary and dragged-out driver eligibility storylines of all time.

Herta needed to rack up 100km in FP1, and avoid any licence penalty points, to get the one bonus superlicence point required to finally hit the threshold he and Cadillac thought he’d reached a week ago in Mexico.

That basically meant 23 laps of Interlagos. Herta’s credited with 31, which is well past the kilometre threshold – although, as Cadillac’s Marc Hynes mentioned, there’s a tiny degree of doubt whether you count only timed laps or just what’s logged in the session.

By our count, Herta managed 23 timed laps that were not inlaps or outlaps, so we reckoned he should be safe. Hynes said 24 was the “sweet spot”, but this just means being absolutely 100% sure either way. 

And Herta avoided any sanction in-session that would deny him the bonus superlicence, after a near-miss not coming into the pits when the session was red flagged because he was too close to the pit entry to react when the panels lit up. Phew!

The FIA subsequently confirmed that Herta’s now all good, so this is now something that everybody, especially him, can stop worrying about... -

Winner: Gabriel Bortoleto’s Audi (8th)

The one Audi that held together all day was rapid, leading the midfield by a couple of tenths and picking off Isack Hadjar’s underperforming Red Bull for good measure.

“The track was quite grippy today, FP2 especially, so quite in a happy place,” reported Gabriel Bortoleto. “I think the car was behaving well, I was driving well today.”

The key of course will be building on that encouraging start through Saturday, when conditions could change, and ensuring the car holds together well enough to avoid another scoring opportunity slipping through Audi’s fingers.

“Honestly, my car has been working OK this weekend, and hopefully it can keep up like this,” Bortoleto added, “and hopefully they fix also Nico's car, because we had a good performance this weekend, I'm sure he can come strong as well.” -

Loser: Nico Hulkenberg's Audi...

There was a bad case of deja vu for Audi where one side of the garage was again beset by reliability trouble.

In Mexico, Bortoleto logged no laps in FP1. In Brazil, it was Nico Hulkenberg’s turn – except he went one ‘better’, completing zero laps at all, all day.

That’s because FP1 stand-in Freddie Slater took over Hulkenberg’s car in the opening session, but ground to a halt with what eventually turned out to be a gearbox problem.

Not only did this ruin Slater’s outing one week after his Mexico FP1 debut was slightly limited by a different problem, it was so complicated to trace that by the time Audi had a handle on the issue it was too late to get everything ready for Hulkenberg to drive in FP2.

Racing director Allan McNish couldn’t hide his frustration. The only silver lining was the seven laps Slater did, he enjoyed, and the team was impressed by, as the 18-year-old has made a good impact with his approach off-track and the quality of the work he’s started to do on it. -

Winner: Haas (10th & 16th)

Ollie Bearman was within two tenths of the lead of the midfield in practice two on Friday, a welcome distraction from Haas's dramatic off-track headline-making with Rafael Camara replacing Esteban Ocon this weekend.

The usual practice caveats apply but 10th is a very handy place for Haas to end its day, although its lack of pace on the hard tyre and the reprimand Camara received for badly impeding Leclerc means this entry has its drawbacks.

But quick on the softs, and with Camara doing "brilliantly" on his first day in the car, there's a silver lining to what was always going to be a tough weekend amid the current turmoil at this team. -

items.title: ‘Dangerous’ but also ‘brilliant’ - Rafael Camara’s F1 debut
items.author: Scott Mitchell-Malm
items.content:
New Haas driver Rafa Camara received a reprimand on his Formula 1 debut for what was deemed “clearly dangerous” impeding of Charles Leclerc in Brazilian Grand Prix practice.

Camara weaved and moved into the racing line as he prepared to start a push lap in FP2 at Interlagos just as Leclerc was coming by to complete a lap of his own.

Though he was warned several times that Leclerc was approaching, Camara ended up squeezing the Ferrari towards the run-off at high speed “with a significantamount of the car off the track”, said the stewards, who upgraded the typical practice penalty for impeding from a warning to a formal reprimand.

“The situation that was created was clearly dangerous and [Camara] should have taken more care to avoid impeding [Leclerc]."

Camara’s incident with Leclerc was a blot on an otherwise solid and steadily improving first day in the car.

He finished 0.86s slower than Ollie Bearman in FP1, and trimmed the gap to 0.57s in FP2, with the biggest part of his time lost in the middle sector - although he had been even closer on the initial hard-tyre push laps before switching to softs.

There was a recurring problem under braking into Turn 1, where Camara had huge run-ending lock-ups in both FP1 and FP2, although several drivers had trouble here.

And he was still trying to smoothen his throttle usage exiting Turns 2 and 12 by the end of Friday as well.

But considering Camara has been thrown in at the deep end with a lot of procedural stuff to learn as well as getting on top of a 2026 car he is driving for the first time, Haas felt he had a “pretty strong day”, head of car engineering Hoagy Nidd said.

“Obviously a massive learning curve today, it's pretty intimidating, but he did brilliantly,” said Nidd.

“He built up steadily through FP1. He was sort of almost a bit reticent to give too much feedback from FP1 and obviously for FP2 he was improving all the time and building with his feedback and his driving, so a pretty strong day I would say.

“Working on procedures, you probably saw us go out, do a few starts, things like that, just the normal bread and butter things that we almost take for granted with most drivers, so we're very pleased with him I think.”

items.title: Wolff backs MotoGP's handling of calendar dissent
items.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
items.content:
Mercedes Formula 1 boss Toto Wolff has backed MotoGP's handling of its Qatar Grand Prix amid rider discontent, ahead of F1's own planned races in the region.

While F1 has gathered at Interlagos for the Brazilian Grand Prix, MotoGP is competing at Qatar's Lusail circuit on the same weekend - with 16 of the 22 full-time riders (and two injury replacements) in action.

This followed several secret and unofficial votes between the MotoGP riders, in which the majority had voted against holding a Qatar race due to fears of conflict escalation in the Middle East.

In the end, though, only the Yamaha riders - those representing the factory team and the satellite team Pramac - are absent from the Qatar GP without replacement.

Yamaha announced last Sunday that it "had not identified sufficient grounds to change its existing company-wide travel restrictions" to send its teams to Qatar, a decision that was met with "disappointment" and suggestion of "sporting consequences" from MotoGP.

The series emphasised it did not "receive any information that would warrant a change to the current plans for the event" after consultation with Qatar, the track and "independent safety advisors".

As for the riders present in Qatar, some have taken a more conciliatory stance over the handling of the event, but others have maintained a more confrontational tone.

Notably, seven-time series champion Marc Marquez said in the pre-event press conference: "I would like to be in another place. For that reason I arrive on the latest flight possible, and I will leave on the earliest flight possible."

F1 has two races scheduled in the region - November 29's Qatar GP, and December 6's Abu Dhabi GP.

And when asked at Interlagos whether his understanding of the situation with those races was being informed with MotoGP racing at Qatar this weekend, Wolff offered an extensive answer that backed MotoGP's approach and questioned what the riders have shared publicly.

"Stefano [Domenicali, F1 boss] and Mohammed [Ben Sulayem, FIA president] have been pretty clear about the situation, that Formula 1 follows what the international guidelines are, whether there's travel restrictions, airlines not flying, any warnings in the region, the kind of feedback that local governments are making - so not only the promoters, but what the local governments are making. And this is what you need to rely on, in my opinion," Wolff said.

"And I'm fully with that. I think that if riders stand up, that geopolitically know nothing about what's going on but [they] have the audience that listens, I think that is something that creates media value [headlines] - but I would have done the same that MotoGP management has done.

"You want to ride, or drive, go. If you don't want to, don't go. As simple as that.

"And everybody can take their personal decisions on that, and I respect it. Of course, you've got to be wary of what's happening in the next few days, or few weeks.

"And Stefano has the finger on the pulse to monitor that. If things were to get more dangerous, then he's going to be the first one, together with Mohammed, to protect the people that were meant to travel. And so that's why I'm following the guidance of what I'm hearing.

"Internally it hasn't been raised, hasn't been a topic. But also there, if someone feels he or she doesn't feel comfortable in travelling, then it's something that I would always respect.

"And maybe that's an opportunity to give somebody else a chance.

"It wouldn't change anything for the relationship. I've always respected that, that some people didn't want to go to certain grands prix. And that's how I see it at the moment."

Crunch time for F1 calendar

Wolff’s comments come ahead of a crunch week for Formula 1 when it comes to defining how the 2026 season will end.

For a while now, Imola has been getting its venue ready as a fallback option in case the final Middle Eastern races cannot happen.

However, it is now at the point where it needs to commit to the final major preparations or abandon its work because the races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi are happening.

It is understood that F1 has set itself a deadline of next Tuesday (November 10) to make a final call on what to do with the Imola event.

If by then it is satisfied that the Middle Eastern races are good to go, then Imola can be stood down.

That call means, however, that if after that date tensions escalate in the Middle East and the races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi have to be halted, then it means Imola will not be able to host any more – which means the season would finish in Las Vegas.

While the situation in the Middle East remains unpredictable, F1 teams retain faith that no "risks" will be taken in the final call.

Aston Martin chief trackside officer Mike Krack said that despite team personnel asking more questions about what was happening, there was confidence in F1’s senior management.

Speaking on Thursday at Interlagos, Krack said: “Now, I discussed it at length with Andy [Stevenson, sporting director] this morning, and we think, we are really convinced, that F1 is not taking any unnecessary risk.

“They are aware of the situation, they have much better information than we have. And I think if there is a serious risk, I think they will take the correct action.

“I think at the moment they are still evaluating that situation, and I’m sure they have set themselves some deadlines, which we have not gone over yet. So, I think we need to give them the time to do that. But I would be really surprised if they take risks.”

items.title: What happened in F1 2026 Brazilian GP second practice
items.author: Scott Mitchell-Malm
items.content:
Kimi Antonelli showed no signs of becoming complacent after his recently-sealed 2026 Formula 1 title win as he completed his domination of Friday practice in Brazil.

Antonelli topped FP2 with a comfortable 0.253s margin ahead of McLaren’s Lando Norris, who headed a gaggle of other cars.

In fact, the gap the lead Mercedes had over a mixed-up cast of would-be contenders at Interlagos reflected how 2026 has tended to play out overall.

Norris, Max Verstappen's Red Bull and George Russell's Mercedes were covered by just 0.020s, while Oscar Piastri was fifth in the second McLaren only half a tenth further back.

Verstappen was once again displeased with some engine behaviour in this session - and his confusion over Red Bull’s slightly vague update on how it was "adapting" to him prompted an amusing radio exchange where Verstappen suggested he should start talking to the clutch directly.

Less funny was the fact he ended the session early in the garage as a steering issue emerged that Red Bull could not quickly resolve.

In performance terms, the outlier at the moment is Ferrari, which seems to be struggling on balance but also (as usual) with straightline speed.

Lewis Hamilton led the team in sixth, nearly three tenths ahead of Charles Leclerc – who survived a high-speed near-miss when F1 debutant Rafa Camara’s Haas inadvertently squeezed him coming onto the start-finish straight.

Camara, who ended his first day as an F1 driver 16th fastest and just over half a second slower than Haas team-mate Ollie Bearman, will be investigated after the session for the incident. 

He was preparing to start a lap when he squeezed Leclerc, who was finishing one, towards the run-off as they navigated the flat-out kink of Turn 15.

Leclerc kept his foot in over the bumpy run-off and managed to finish the lap, losing a couple of tenths in the process, and expressed his irritation afterwards.

These were Leclerc’s first laps of the weekend after Dino Beganovic drove his car in FP1.

Early on Leclerc complained that the balance was too far to the rear, and at the end of the session he was asking about the engine.

Towards the foot of the top 10, Gabriel Bortoleto was eighth in his Audi on home soil, just over a second off Antonelli but ahead of Isack Hadjar's Red Bull.

Ollie Bearman's Haas completed the top 10 but there was just half a tenth covering him, Franco Colapinto's Alpine and the Racing Bulls of Arvid Lindblad and Liam Lawson.

The only driver not to set a time was Nico Hulkenberg, who did not run at all after the issue that stopped Freddie Slater on track in FP1 could not be addressed by Audi in time, leaving Hulkenberg without a single lap in the car on Friday.

For those who did drive, there was a recurring challenge for almost everybody: lock-ups into the first corner.

At least half the field had a big moment under braking for the Senna S, struggling with the bumps as the track falls away, which could be a precursor to a defining performance differentiator come qualifying on Saturday.

items.title: What we learned about Ferrari's key Hamilton/Leclerc meeting
items.author: Jon Noble
items.content:
Ferrari boss Fred Vasseur wasted little time following his arrival into Sao Paulo on Thursday night in getting his Formula 1 drivers together for their well-publicised Mexican Grand Prix postmortem.

Fresh off his own arrival from Italy, and with Charles Leclerc having also flown in from Monaco where he had returned for the birth of his first child, the pair of them got together with Lewis Hamilton at their downtown hotel.

Away from the prying eyes of journalists and photographs, the three of them ran through the events of that opening lap in Mexico, were Vasseur told them his views on events and then agreed a path going forward that it is hoped will avoid a repeat clash in the future.

Speaking in the team principals' press conference on Friday, Vasseur adopting his usual tone of wanting to keep things "private" when he appeared in front of the media.

His tone of answering throughout was very much of keeping details close to his chest for what he now considers a closed matter.

"It went well," he said about the meeting. "It was good to discuss, good to clarify my position and their position. It was good to do. Now we turn the page and we are focused on the next one."

But while Vasseur was not expansive in terms of details from the meetings, there were still some clear hints about where the situation stands now after Mexico.

The major one is that there has been no significant change of approach from Vasseur in terms of the capacity for both his drivers to race each other hard.

Vasseur has long shied away from any desire to interfere in the on-track battles – which has sometimes been equally frustrating for one or both of his drivers.

But Vasseur did state that the racing guidelines that his team operate to – even without formal rules of engagement – were unchanged.

"The guidelines are still the same," said Vasseur. "I think they accumulated perhaps a bit of frustration because they are starting each weekend side by side and you have a kind of accumulation of facts. But at the end of the day, the guidelines are always the same."

Vasseur repeatedly referenced that key to the guidelines being followed was not letting personal interests overtake those of the team and that this "message was clear" for both Hamilton and Leclerc.

Referencing this later he said: "They are working for the team and the team has to come first. In this situation, we failed collectively because we were 1-2 and we didn't win the race in the end. It's clear that we failed and we have to react.

"The conclusion of the meeting yesterday evening was clear. It was a clear reminder that Ferrari is coming first. It's coming first for the brand, for the employees, for the tifosi and this we have to keep in mind."

Vasseur sat in the press conference alongside Mercedes boss Toto Wolff, who interrupted at one point to reference that what Ferrari was living through now felt like a repeat of the headaches he faced with Hamilton and Nico Rosberg during their title fight years of 2014 to 2016.

Wolff suggested that difficult moments like Mexico for Ferrari were important in exposing weaknesses in the system, and, like the 2016 Spanish GP for Mercedes, often became a catalyst for allowing change to happen.

He explained: "I think sometimes it needs the really tough ones, like the last one, to make a point.

"It was always when I was there with Nico and Lewis, when there was an accident, it was understood that that was now the limit and it wouldn't continue like this.

"That's why maybe it needed to escalate to the point, because it's a respect to the team and many, many thousand people, the brand, that work together and that's what they need to keep in their heads."

But while Wolff was quite open during those years about how he was laying down the law with his drivers – which included him stating at one point that he would sack one of his drivers if they could not race each other cleanly - Vasseur’s approach is much more secretive.

"I'm not sure that Toto, 10 years ago, told you exactly the content of the discussion with Nico and Lewis and I will do exactly the same," said Vasseur, who perhaps had not recalled Wolff’s openness at the time.

"We had a discussion. It has to stay private, it's a matter of respect also for them and for the team. And once again the most important is the message.

"The message is that we are working for a brand, we are working for sponsors, we are working for, but I would say mainly also the employees of the team."

Vasseur did not see any cause for alarm in how the relationship of his two drivers stands, but may have offered a hint that he was not impressed with how Hamilton had spoken strongly after Mexico.

Asked about any concerns in Hamilton saying he would "not be silenced" based on what was said after Mexico, Vasseur said: "No, no – but this I was clear with Lewis and I will keep it between Lewis and me."

Vasseur certainly countered Hamilton’s suggestion that Leclerc races the seven-time champion harder than any other drivers on the grid – citing his opening lap move on Max Verstappen in Austin as proof of him being super aggressive with other teams.

"If you have a look at what Charles did in Austin in the first section, everybody said that it was magic and the line is fine between the two," said Vasseur.

However, he acknowledged that a rivalry between his drivers was to be expected and it was naïve to think the pair of them could battle like they did and be best buddies.

"I'm not asking them to be best friends," said Vasseur. "I think it would be even probably a bit negative. I'm just asking them to act and to work as professionals and this is it."

Despite repeated questions over a topic that Vasseur would have loved not to have cropped up in the first place, he acknowledged that there were downsides to having two top line drivers battling each other in the same team.

However, he felt that it would be hard to enjoy the benefits that come from having a pairing like Hamilton and Leclerc without expecting there to be any negatives.

"I think it’s probably the downside of the system is that we have two competitive guys starting each weekend next to each other," he explained.

"But I think if we are P2 [in the constructors’ championship] today, it’s also because we have two guys very, very close and we have to manage it.

"But it’s a choice, it’s a choice in the line-up and I have the positive and the negative. I will deal with the negative."

items.title: Surprise Ducati pacesetter on Qatar MotoGP Friday
items.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
items.content:
VR46 Ducati rider Fabio Di Giannantonio set the pace to end Friday practice at the Qatar Grand Prix, delivering a new record lap in the process.

Di Giannantonio led points leader Marc Marquez by 0.142s in a Ducati 1-2. The Italian is a known Lusail specialist, having taken the first of his two MotoGP wins at the track back in 2023. 

Marco Bezzecchi (Aprilia) and a resurgent Pecco Bagnaia (Ducati) completed the top four. Bezzecchi's three Aprilia peers - Raul Fernandez, Jorge Martin and Ai Ogura - all secured automatic Q2 spots within the top 10, too, though it was a close call for Ogura.

Other direct spots in Q2 were picked up by Enea Bastianini (Tech3 KTM), Johann Zarco (LCR Honda) and Brad Binder (KTM).

For once, Pedro Acosta had no answer to his fellow KTMs and was only 14th. He now faces the possibility of being outqualified by a team-mate for the first time ever in MotoGP, should he fail to advance from Q1 on Saturday.

It was a notably credible first day as a Honda MotoGP rider for Jake Dixon, standing in for Joan Mir.

Dixon lapped 1.987s off the pace in the end, just two tenths back from out-of-sorts LCR Honda regular Diogo Moreira.

items.title: What happened in first Brazil F1 practice
items.author: Josh Suttill
items.content:
Lando Norris edged the new Formula 1 world champion Kimi Antonelli to top the first practice session at the Brazilian Grand Prix, as Colton Herta completed his F1 superlicence mission.

Norris set the pace with a 1m11.717s, lapping just 0.082s quicker than Antonelli.

McLaren is the only team that has brought upgrades to Brazil with a new front and rear wing, modified floor furniture and a beam wing.

Max Verstappen (Red Bull), who complained of "unacceptable downshifts", and Lewis Hamilton (Ferrari) made it four different teams in the top four, all within just over three tenths of a second.

George Russell was fifth fastest ahead of Isack Hadjar's Red Bull.

Gabriele Mini was the fastest of the six FP1-only rookies in seventh place for Alpine in his second successive FP1 outing, 0.852s off the pace and just under a tenth ahead of regular driver Franco Colapinto, who was ninth.

On home soil, Gabriel Bortoleto's Audi was eighth between the two Alpine drivers while Liam Lawson rounded out the top 10 for Racing Bulls.

McLaren's reserve driver Leonardo Fornaroli was 11th ahead of Haas's Ollie Bearman and Aston Martin's Fernando Alonso.

Rafael Camara finished his first FP1 session in 18th place, eight and a half tenths behind Bearman, as he builds up slowly to his unexpected grand prix debut this weekend - replacing Esteban Ocon.

Herta picked up the final point he needs to qualify for his F1 superlicence, as he surpassed the 100 kilometres of running required to earn the 40th and final point, when combined with his four other qualifying FP1 runs and his IndyCar results.

Cadillac thought it was mission accomplished in Mexico until it emerged that its FIA-verified calculations included an error on IndyCar's website. That meant Herta needed another FP1 outing in Brazil to finally get him over the line, removing a key obstacle to him replacing Valtteri Bottas in 2027, should the team decide to do so.

Bottas was 15th, and nine tenths quicker than Herta in FP1.

Freddie Slater's second FP1 outing ended up being even shorter than his first, as he'd completed just seven laps before his Audi ground to a halt, bringing out an early red flag.

It means Slater has been able to complete just 21 laps between his back-to-back first F1 practice outings in Mexico and Brazil.

Ferrari's Dino Beganovic also had a disrupted FP1 session as he lost a lot of time to his team needing to change his floor mid-session. He ended up with just 11 laps, having been told to abort his soft tyre lap for a car problem.

items.title: What’s happening with Cadillac F1 buyout talks amid Fenway interest
items.author: Darren Cox
items.content:
Once upon a time, if you wanted to know who was buying into a Formula 1 team you could ask the bloke who owned it over coffee in the paddock.

Such is the way ownerships are now structured and managed in F1 there may only be one person in the paddock that actually knows something about the sale, someone with a freshly signed contract who appears to have let something slip on Thursday.

When I recently dug into who actually owns each F1 team, the distance we have travelled from the owner-operator days became very clear. The person running the team, the company whose name is above the garage, and the people who ultimately control the money can be three very different things.

That matters when considering the potential sale of a stake in Cadillac's F1 team.

There has been plenty of talk around the Austin and Mexico paddocks. But the reporting that has moved the story forward has come from American sporting and financial circles, led by Sportico, followed by the likes of the Wall Street Journal. The Race's journalists have been seeking confirmation in Brazil. That does not mean the answers are in Brazil.

I have been told that these negotiations are being handled personally by Walter and a very small circle around him. People working at Silverstone, at the American facilities, or in the garage at Interlagos, could quite reasonably know very little about it.

Cadillac has a struggling racing team and urgent challenges on track to resolve. Its owner has a collection of businesses and challenges of his own to manage, including federal investigations involving his insurance businesses.

That is why Cadillac's stance that nothing has doesn’t mean that nothing is .

My sources have indicated, for months, that a sale process is under way. Getting formal confirmation or anyone willing to speak on the record has proved rather harder, as is often the way with these things. The remaining question is what the outcome of that process will be. That is where the interest lies.

The least surprising part is that somebody wants to buy in.

Fenway among the prospective buyers

Walter has meanwhile been selling sporting assets, including his interests in the Lakers and Chelsea, against the backdrop of reported financial pressures and federal investigations involving his insurance businesses. TWG denies wrongdoing. That wider situation matters far more to this transaction than Cadillac's latest qualifying position.

It does not follow that Walter needed to begin by putting up a "for sale" sign. Prospective investors have been knocking on his door. In his circumstances, those conversations would be difficult to ignore.

The Guardian has reported talks about a majority purchase by Fenway Sports Group, which owns Liverpool FC and the Boston Red Sox among others. The preference on Walter's side appears to be a minority sale that allows him to retain control.

A preference is not a completed deal. But the distinction matters.

Lawrence Stroll provides a useful example. As we explored in the ownership article, he has brought successive investors into Aston Martin while retaining commanding voting and governance rights. Economic ownership and control are different things.

An owner can take money off the table, bring in another investor and still decide who sits in his second F1 seat.

So, the percentage sold will tell only part of Cadillac's story. The rights attached to those shares may tell us considerably more.

It is generally understood that Walter holds 67%, Dan Towriss 3% and General Motors 30%. Those figures have not been publicly confirmed and they do not tell us what approvals or protections GM has.

That is a significant unknown.

When I interviewed Flavio Briatore about Otro Capital's proposed sale of its 24% Alpine stake, he made a practical point about Renault's position. Its formal veto period ran until September. But who would commit hundreds of millions of dollars to a minority stake without a workable relationship with the majority shareholder?

A date passing on a contract does not remove the need to get along.

GM's position at Cadillac is different and we should not assume identical rights. But any buyer would need to understand its relationship with the manufacturer whose name, investment and long-term commitment are central to the proposition.

Seemingly well-informed in such matters, Sergio Perez offered a reminder of that in Brazil on Thursday, speaking to media including The Race.

Perez pointed to GM as "one of the biggest manufacturers", before considering whether the TWG investors wanted to "get some of their investment back".

"But I don't think it will change any structure at all," he said.

Having just signed a new long-term contract, Perez would have had every reason to ask what a sale might mean for the team before committing. He sounds unsure about why the investors would sell, but rather more certain about what happens afterwards. He may know more than most in Brazil. And that last line may have just let it show.

Naturally, there are plenty of other people being linked to said new structure.

An apprentice mechanic's job could become available in F1 and somebody would mention Christian Horner. His name appearing in this conversation is therefore hardly a revelation.

More interestingly I have also heard considerably wilder suggestions involving prominent paddock figures. As far as I can establish, those have not developed into firm outcomes. Yet.

Of the names reported, Fenway Sports Group, I've been assured, looks the most likely to progress.

Why Fenway's interest deserves attention

The very American nature of Fenway is of particular interest.

Informally, GM and senior management have been very pleased with the particularly strong response when Cadillac leans into its American identity. That has strengthened the appetite for an American driver, with Colton Herta increasingly central to that ambition, and for an American investment partner. The Race's audience data backs up this assertion. Our US audience figures spike on Cadillac and Herta stories. Obvious but important.

The process of getting Herta into F1 has, in my view, exposed the inexperience around the decision-making at a sporting level within the team. That deserves a piece of its own, which I will return to if, as seems increasingly likely, he is confirmed around the Las Vegas Grand Prix as Cadillac's second driver for 2027. For now, the decision remains publicly unresolved and Valtteri Bottas has been told there is still a route to him staying.

The commercial logic is easy enough to see. An American manufacturer, an American driver, and an investor experienced in American sport make a coherent proposition to sponsors and supporters.

Herta would still have to deliver behind the wheel. But the appeal of that combination helps explain why the driver discussion and the ownership discussion belong in the same article.

For Walter, the task is now to realise as much value while preserving as much influence as possible. For GM, it is to ensure the funding and stability is in place to support its long-term ambitions.

The negotiations that settle those questions will tell us more about Cadillac's future than anything said outside its garage this weekend.

items.title: McLaren's 2027 F1 front wing breaks cover in Brazil
items.author: Jon Noble
items.content:
McLaren’s new front wing, which will be the same concept it launches its 2027 Formula 1 car with, has been revealed at the Brazilian Grand Prix.

As part of an end-of-season push by the Woking-based squad to deliver continuous improvements to its MCL40, the squad has brought its latest upgrades to Interlagos.

This includes tweaks to its floor, an updated rear wing, but also a front wing that will form the starting point for next season’s MCL41.

The front wing is a change of concept for the team as it features many revisions across the spectrum of wing elements.

The attachment point for the main plane and the endplate has been revised to now run across the lower edge – where it marries up with the refined outboard element.

The attachment between the nose and the main plane has been adjusted to sit on the second flap now rather than the mainplane, while the new wing also features an adjustment in the height of the flap elements.

Speaking ahead of the weekend, McLaren explained that the changes delivered were about both delivering more downforce and improving car balance.

Chief technical officer of aerodynamics Peter Prodromou also made clear that these changes were the launchpad for its 2027 project.

“The season isn't over yet: these upgrades are designed to improve the car now and help us in our fight for third in the championship,” he explained.

“While the learning we take from these upgrades will feed into next year’s development, we also expect to carry over the concept of the new front wing into the launch specification of next year’s car.”

items.title: Marquez quickest as Qatar MotoGP weekend kicks off
items.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
items.content:
MotoGP championship leader Marc Marquez led the way in the opening practice session of the Qatar Grand Prix, heading Marco Bezzecchi by a tenth of a second.

Marquez led virtually the entire session on the dusty Lusail track, and ended up on a 1m52.278s. He never fitted a spare rear tyre - but neither did virtually anyone else, with no incentive to use up any of the valuable rubber in the less-representative daytime session (compared to Friday afternoon practice, the sprint and the grand prix all taking place in the evening under the lights).

Fabio Di Giannantonio was third behind Marquez and Bezzecchi, four tenths down on the leader.

Pedro Acosta was fourth as the lead KTM, but his RC16 seemed to either fail or run out of fuel in the end as he had to pull over to the side of the track.

Jorge Martin, who had withdrawn from the Sepang weekend last time out due to his wrist fracture from Phillip Island, had a livelier start here, logging 16 laps and placing fifth.

With the Yamaha riders absent as the manufacturer elected to skip Qatar, a total of 18 riders took part. Honda's new stand-in Jake Dixon was last of them, after crashing on his very first flying lap.

But Dixon was just 3.1s off the pace in the end, so will have zero trouble clearing MotoGP's 105-percent pace rule for race eligibility.

There was another crash early in the session, for KTM's Brad Binder, who likewise returned to action shortly.

items.title: How much has bad luck really cost George Russell in F1 2026?
items.author: Josh Suttill
items.content:
George Russell says he's only had six race weekends without an issue in a bruising 2026 Formula 1 season.

But, on a Brazilian Grand Prix weekend where he's facing another grid penalty, does his claim stack up, and how much does bad luck explain his clear defeat to Kimi Antonelli? 

Antonelli has destroyed his Mercedes team-mate Russell this year, winning nine races to Russell's three and wrapping up the title with four rounds to spare last weekend in Mexico.

Facing the media for the first time in Brazil since that crushing title loss was confirmed, Russell admitted to "feel[ing] a bit exhausted this season of constantly picking myself back up". 

"When you get kicked to the ground, you pick yourself back up, then you get kicked down again, you pick yourself back up, and I was hoping to do that maybe twice in the season, not every other weekend really," he said. 

"When you get to a point of this season, you're away from home three weeks in a row, and you have another race like what happened in Mexico, where a chance of victory, a chance of the podium, just disappears totally outside of your control, it's tough to deal with. It's very tough to deal with. 

"So Brazil's a place that I love, I've got great memories of. Do I come in with high expectations? Honestly, no, to be honest. But looking forward to next year for sure. And just continue to work on the things that I can control, and pray that things outside of my control sort themselves out." 

Russell said he went through every race of 2026 with his engineers and found "we've only had six races this season where we had not an issue". 

"So 14 [likely 13, as there have been 19 weekends so far] of those races we've had things that have been what we thought was bad luck, but we need to start questioning things more deeply when it's happening so often, and especially on our side. 

"That was the main feeling for me." 

So, we put that claim to the test: we've gone through F1 2026's 19 weekends so far and found the following:

Russell's campaign started in dream fashion with a dominant victory in the Australian season opener, while Antonelli paid the price for a costly final practice crash that left him compromised for the rest of the weekend on a suboptimal, unrefined set-up. 

He could probably still count Australia as an 'issue' weekend as he had to fight back from having a depleted battery before he started the race - costing him positions to the Ferraris and requiring him to fight back into the lead.

Russell followed it up with a sprint win in China, but his first real bit of bad luck came in grand prix qualifying when his car ground to a halt at the start of Q3. This left him needing a late lap to salvage second on the grid. 

Reflecting on that session, Russell told media including The Times: "I pulled the clutch half a second too early in the qualifying, which led to my car breaking down. 

"Should we have known about that? Maybe yes. Maybe not." 

Russell had been faster than Antonelli all the way through the weekend up to that point, so you can make a case he'd have won there with a normal Q3. 

At Suzuka, poor safety car timing helped Antonelli to victory and cost Russell a shot at it. But Antonelli looked the faster driver and may have won on sheer pace. It looked more like a fight between him and Oscar Piastri's McLaren.

But Russell was also then further compromised on the safety car restart by his car being put into an extra harvesting mode, leaving him fourth at the chequered flag. 

"Then in Japan, doing the upshift at the exact same time as I clicked another button...on the steering wheel...should we have known about that? Maybe yes. Maybe not," Russell reflected. 

Antonelli won from pole in Miami while Russell finished fourth on what appeared to be a clean weekend for both cars.

Russell and Antonelli then scrapped for victory in Canada when Russell's engine failed while he was leading. 

Antonelli won again in Monaco while Russell had a double-hit of penalties, the latter for Mercedes not serving his first, a five-second penalty for pitlane speeding, correctly. 

Given the circumstances of the pitlane speed limit penalties that weekend and Russell being blameless for the second penalty, it was another unlucky weekend and a lost podium (as he was third on the late-race restart). 

Russell finished second at Barcelona; Antonelli had passed him (and may have challenged Lewis Hamilton for the victory), but his Mercedes broke down with an electrical issue late on.

Russell won in Austria, beautifully judging the yellow flags in qualifying while Antonelli mistook double-waved yellows for single ones and backed off, ending up fourth on the grid and third in the race. 

Russell struggled with power unit deployment issues at Silverstone and Spa. At Silverstone he salvaged second (so probably did not lose any points) while Antonelli loses a likely victory to a front-left wheel-shield failure. At Spa, the issue cost Russell 0.2-0.25 seconds in qualifying, while on the opening lap it left him vulnerable on the Kemmel Straight. 

This led to contact with Lewis Hamilton, who was penalised for the collision - which put Russell out on the spot. Antonelli won the race from pole. 

At Hungary, Russell cracked a sump running slightly wide over a kerb in Q3, which left him seventh on the grid prompted engine-swap ramifications down the line. Then in the race he stalled and sank like a stone because of an engine rev anomaly, and an ill-timed virtual safety car stunted his recovery, while Antonelli took third. 

Antonelli and Russell finished second and third at Zandvoort, while at Monza Antonelli's excellent charge through the field - from 19th, owing to an engine-change grid penalty - was aided by the red flag and another well-timed virtual safety car.  

Antonelli's pace was so strong he may have still won without those anyway, but he was certainly aided by fortune on Sunday. 

A virtual safety car helped Antonelli beat Lando Norris's McLaren to victory in Madrid while Russell was fifth, off Antonelli's pace all weekend. 

Russell won in Baku while Antonelli crashed in qualifying before recovering to fifth. 

Another power unit failure at Sepang cost Russell a likely podium meant he had to take a grid penalty in Singapore. Russell blew a sprint victory there by crashing out of the lead at the end of the first lap, while he recovered to ninth in the grand prix.

Russell picked up a five-second time penalty for leaving the track and gaining an advantage at Austin and labelled his own pace "rubbish" en route to eighth, while Antonelli won again.

Then in Antonelli's title-sealing Mexico weekend, Russell had a deployment issue that dropped him from his front-row start. He clashed with Isack Hadjar's Red Bull and was penalised 10 seconds. 

So really, there have been 12 weekends where Russell has some publicly disclosed bad luck - 10 of which cost him points - not counting issues that he or the team have not revealed. It is true that this dwarfs Antonelli's misfortune, as he only really lost points to factors outside his control at Silverstone and Barcelona.   

Ultimately, Russell can only make a case that he lost victories in China (Q3 problem), Canada (power unit failure) and Monza (red flag and VSC timing that helped Antonelli), but even all three of those were far from guaranteed. Maybe Antonelli would've just been quicker even if Russell had a normal qualifying in China, maybe Antonelli would've won their dogfight in Canada, and maybe Antonelli had the pace at Monza to win regardless.

We'll never know the answer to those questions, but only the most ludicrously generous estimates of the points Russell has lost this season put him marginally ahead of Antonelli right now, if you then subtract the points Antonelli gains from it.

Russell's lost points to bad luck - A (very) generous view

China - 7 points (1st not 2nd) Japan - 6 points (2nd not 4th)

Montreal - 25 points (1st not DNF) 

Monaco - 15 points (3rd not 12th) 

Belgium - 15 points (3rd not DNF) 

Hungary - 6 points (4th not 7th)

Italy - 7 points (1st not 2nd) 

Malaysia - 15 points (3rd not 20th) 

Singapore - 6 points (6th not 9th) 

Mexico - 10 points (2nd not 6th) 

Total = 112 lost points New gap to Antonelli = Russell leads by 6 points 

*accounting for Antonelli's net points loss as a result

This would be an impossibly fortunate season for Russell, taking very generous liberties such as assuming he wins in China, Canada and Italy, plus presuming he maintains his second place in Mexico, and crucially not removing of Antonelli's own bad luck.

And even in this highly unlikely scenario where Russell is leading by six points, you'd back Antonelli to overturn it comfortably in the final four races on this season's form. 

In reality, even if you balanced out the reliability dramas of both cars, of which Russell has had more, Russell would still be over 60 points behind Antonelli instead of 130. 

Russell called it "difficult to put a number on how much [reliability] has impacted the championship" and pointed to one important factor. 

"It's often about momentum. When we start the season, we had the issue in China with the failure in qualifying, we had the issues in Japan, we had the engine failure in Canada, we had the drivethrough penalty that wasn't a drivethrough penalty in Monaco. These things compound," Russell explained.

"If you're in the championship fight, or you're within touching distance, you don't feel like you're having to do catch-up. And maybe that contributed towards overdriving and trying to overachieve. Maybe not." 

Again, we'll never know how a cleaner start to the season would've changed things for Russell or put more pressure on Antonelli. Russell's bigger problem was how quickly Antonelli became the faster Mercedes driver. 

Has Russell had more bad luck than Antonelli this year? Yes. But has Antonelli been the better, faster driver on more weekends? Absolutely yes. 

And it's something Russell himself acknowledged in Mexico on the eve of Antonelli's coronation: "The truth is he's been at a higher level than me this year."

The bad luck ballooned the gap and made the defeat all the more crushing, but the speed and execution difference this year meant the intra-team fight was only ever going one way.

items.title: Russell to take grid penalty at F1's Brazilian GP
items.author: Josh Suttill
items.content:
George Russell will take a five-place grid penalty for this weekend's Formula 1 Brazilian Grand Prix for a new internal combustion engine, his second grid drop in four races.

Russell had a 60-place grid penalty for a suite of power unit component changes in Singapore last month, a necessity after he retired with a power unit failure in Malaysia the week before.

He knew then that he would have to take another grid penalty before the end of the year, and Mercedes has chosen Brazil to do so at Interlagos this weekend, with Russell confirming the decision on Mercedes' Instagram account.

"We always had to take a grid penalty at some point between Singapore and the end of the season," Russell explained.

"We felt like this was a good place to take it. Lewis [Hamilton] had a big grid penalty here a number of years ago [in 2021] and did pretty well.

"Five places doesn't seem that bad and we’ll try to come back through."

Driving for Mercedes in 2021, Hamilton was disqualified after topping sprint qualifying for a technical non-conformity (a misaligned DRS), yet charged from 20th to fifth in the sprint.

Back then, the sprint result dictated your start position for the grand prix but, after taking a new internal combustion engine, Hamilton was dropped back to 10th on the grid.

He still comfortably won the grand prix from there.

So Brazil is a logical choice for Russell to take the engine penalty, one that was originally going to coincide with the debut of Mercedes' Additional Development and Upgrade Opportunities-assisted (ADUO) engine.

But the debut of that ADUO engine is uncertain, and there's no guarantee it will appear before the end of the season, with a maximum of three races remaining after Brazil.

Mercedes does not want to rush its introduction and will only introduce it when it is sure it is ready, with the drivers' championship already sealed and the constructors' championship all but guaranteed.
